lines.text: Bram had started building beacons while I was in Aldcrown. A tower every ten miles, from Saltmouth to the Senn, so the north could talk to itself in fire.
Four were finished when Penhallow came. By the third week of the Winter War, there were thirty.
One fire means look. Two means trouble. Three means a great deal of trouble.
And four?
Four means somebody's cooking on the beacon again, and I'll have his ears.

We tested it on a clear night. Bram lit one fire on the keep. Ten miles away, a second tower answered. Then a third. Then a line of tiny lights ran away south across the dark, all the way to the river.
Four days later, a rider from the Senn galloped in to say they'd seen it. The fire had taken one hour.
Then Ysolde took the beacons away from Bram.
A beacon line is a road, Lord Lucan. Roads carry bread. If you mean to fight a war across three hundred miles of snow, someone has to count the bread.
So I made her quartermaster of the north. It was the easiest decision of the war. Halvard was terrified of her, which helped.
In her first week, she found eleven sacks of barley that Kesting's men had lost. They were under Halvard's bed.
My lord. Lady Ysolde asks why our arrows cost a copper more than Marrick's.
And why do they?
Because ours hit things, my lord.
Corvin and Ysolde argued about money every day for a month. By the end of it, the north had the best-run army in Aldmere, and the two of them were friends without either one noticing.
At night I'd climb the beacon tower on the keep and look at the line of dark towers running south. Every one of them was a family who had agreed to sit up all winter, watching for fire.
You keep counting them, my lord.
Thirty towers. A hundred and twenty people. If the army comes, they're the first to see it. And the first it reaches.
They know. They asked for the job. That's all a line is, my lord. People deciding to stand in a row.
Down in the village, someone was singing. In the hall, the lamp burned white. And the towers stood dark against the snow, all the way to the river.
Then, at the very end of the line, far to the south, a tiny light came on.
Then a second, beside it.
Then a third.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and twenty-five, coming soon.
